claim: A single mechanism of loop extrusion by condensins can robustly compact, segregate and disentangle chromosomes, arriving at individualized chromatids with morphology observed in vivo.
source: Using polymer simulations of chromosome dynamics, we show that a single mechanism of loop extrusion by condensins can robustly compact, segregate and disentangle chromosomes, arriving at individualized chromatids with morphology observed in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by polymer simulation data presented throughout the manuscript, including Figures 2 and 3 and associated videos.

claim: Eukaryote chromosomes are condensed into elongated structures that maintain linear order.
source: First, the chromosomes are condensed into elongated structures that maintain the linear order, i.e. the order of genomic elements in the elongated chromosome resembles their order along the genome (Trask et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Trask et al., 1993.

claim: The compaction machinery distinguishes different chromosomes and chromatids, preferentially forming intra-chromatid cross-links.
source: Second, the compaction machinery is able to distinguish different chromosomes and chromatids, preferentially forming intra-chromatid cross-links: if this were not the case, segregation would not occur (Nasmyth, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nasmyth, 2001 and logical inference about segregation requirements.

claim: The process of compaction is coincident with segregation of sister chromatids.
source: Third, the process of compaction is coincident with segregation of sister chromatids, i.e. formation of two separate chromosomal bodies.
evidence: This is stated as an established observation about chromosome behavior.

claim: Originally intertwined sister chromatids become topologically disentangled during compaction.
source: Finally, originally intertwined sister chromatids become topologically disentangled, which is surprising, given the general tendency of polymers to become more intertwined as they are concentrated (Marko, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Marko, 2011 and contrasted with general polymer physics knowledge.

claim: Indiscriminate cross-linking of chromosomes cannot produce the features of chromosome compaction observed during mitosis.
source: None of these features cannot be produced by indiscriminate cross-linking of chromosomes (Marko and Siggia, 1997), which suggests that a novel mechanism of polymer compaction must occur, namely 'lengthwise compaction' (Marko, 2009; 2011; Marko and Rippe, 2011), which permits each chromatid to be compacted while avoiding sticking of separate chromatids together.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Marko and Siggia, 1997 and subsequent papers on lengthwise compaction.

claim: Topoisomerase II and condensin are essential for metaphase chromosome compaction.
source: Cell-biological studies suggest that topoisomerase II and condensin are essential for metaphase chromosome compaction (Hirano and Mitchison, 1993; 1994; Wood and Earnshaw, 1990; Hirano, 1995), leading to the hypothesis that mitotic compaction-segregation relies on the interplay between the activities of these two protein complexes.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Mitotic chromosomes consist of arrays of consecutive loops.
source: Final structures of mitotic chromosomes were shown to consist arrays of consecutive loops (Paulson and Laemmli, 1977; Earnshaw and Laemmli, 1983; Naumova et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental observations.

claim: Loop extrusion creates an array of consecutive loops in individual chromosomes.
source: This 'loop extrusion' process creates an array of consecutive loops in individual chromosomes (Nasmyth, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Nasmyth, 2001.

claim: Loop extrusion dynamics has two regimes: a sparse regime with little compaction and a dense regime with efficient compaction.
source: Simulations of this system at larger scales (Goloborodko et al., 2015) have established that there are two regimes of the steady-state dynamics: (i) a sparse regime where little compaction is achieved and, (ii) a dense regime where a dense array of stabilized loops efficiently compacts a chromosome.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior simulation work by Goloborodko et al., 2015.

claim: Loop extrusion in the dense regime generates chromatin loops that are stabilized by multiple stacked condensins.
source: Importantly, loop extrusion in the dense regime generates chromatin loops that are stabilized by multiple "stacked" condensins (Alipour and Marko, 2012), making loops robust against the known dynamic binding-unbinding of individual condensin complexes (Gerlich et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Alipour and Marko, 2012 and Gerlich et al., 2006.

claim: Each monomer in the simulation corresponds to three nucleosomes (600 bp).
source: We consider a chromosome as a flexible polymer, coarse-graining to monomers of 10 nm diameter, each corresponding to three nucleosomes (600 bp).
evidence: This is a model parameter definition stated in the Methods section.

claim: The polymer has a persistence length of ~5 monomers (3 Kb).
source: As earlier (Naumova et al., 2013; Fudenberg et al., 2015), the polymer has a persistence length of ~5 monomers (3 Kb), is subject to excluded volume interactions and to the activity of loop-extruding condensin molecules and topo II (see below, and in Fudenberg et al. (2015)).
evidence: This is a model parameter based on prior work cited.

claim: The simulations use chains of 50000 monomers, corresponding to 30 Mb.
source: We simulate chains of 50000 monomers, which corresponds to 30 Mb, close to the size of the smallest human chromosomal arm.
evidence: This is a model parameter stated in the Methods section.

claim: Only one condensin is permitted to bind to each monomer, modeling steric exclusion.
source: As in prior lattice models of condensins (Goloborodko et al., 2015; Alipour and Marko, 2012), when two condensins collide on the chromatin, their translocation is blocked; equivalently, only one condensin is permitted to bind to each monomer, modeling their steric exclusion.
evidence: This is a model rule based on prior work cited.

claim: Loop extrusion by condensins and strand passing mediated by topo II convert initially globular interphase chromosomes into elongated, unknotted structures that resemble prophase chromosomes.
source: Our main qualitative result is that loop extrusion by condensins and strand passing mediated by topo II convert initially globular interphase chromosomes into elongated, unknotted and relatively stiff structures that closely resemble prophase chromosomes (Figure 2, Video 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2, Video 2, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Compacted chromosomes have the 'noodle' morphology of prophase chromosomes observed in optical and electron microscopy.
source: The compacted chromosomes have the familiar 'noodle' morphology (Figure 2BC) of prophase chromosomes observed in optical and electron microscopy (Yunis, 1981; Sumner, 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data in Figure 2BC and citations to experimental observations.

claim: Simulated chromosomes preserve the underlying linear order of the genome.
source: Consistent with the observed linear organization of prophase chromosomes, our simulated chromosomes preserve the underlying linear order of the genome (Yunis, 1981; Sumner, 1991; Yunis and Sanchez, 1975; Furey and Haussler, 2003; Strukov and Belmont, 2009) (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data in Figure 2C and citations to experimental observations.

claim: Simulated and human chromosomes have the linear compaction density of ~5 kb/nm.
source: Moreover, the geometric parameters of our simulated chromosomes match the experimentally measured parameters of mid-prophase chromosomes Figure 2—figure supplement 1: both simulated and human chromosomes have the linear compaction density of ~5 kb/nm (Yunis, 1981) and the radius of 300 nm (el-Alfy and Leblond, 1989; Sarkar et al., 2002; Kireeva et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citation to Yunis, 1981.

claim: Simulated and human chromosomes have a radius of 300 nm.
source: Moreover, the geometric parameters of our simulated chromosomes match the experimentally measured parameters of mid-prophase chromosomes Figure 2—figure supplement 1: both simulated and human chromosomes have the linear compaction density of ~5 kb/nm (Yunis, 1981) and the radius of 300 nm (el-Alfy and Leblond, 1989; Sarkar et al., 2002; Kireeva et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citations to experimental measurements.

claim: Chromosome compaction proceeds by two stages: fast formation of a loose, elongated morphology, followed by a slow maturation stage.
source: Second, simulations show that chromosome compaction proceeds by two stages (Figure 2AB): fast formation of a loose, elongated morphology, followed by a slow maturation stage.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2AB.

claim: During the initial 'loop formation stage', condensins associate with the chromosome and extrude loops until colliding with each other, rapidly compacting the chromosome.
source: During the initial 'loop formation stage', condensins associate with the chromosome and extrude loops until colliding with each other, rapidly compacting the chromosome (Figure 2, Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2 and Video 2.

claim: The loop formation stage takes a fraction of the condensin exchange time.
source: At the end of this stage, that takes a fraction of the condensin exchange time, a gapless array of loops is formed, the loops are relatively small, supported by single condensins, and the chromosome is long and thin (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: During the maturation stage, due to condensin exchange some loops dissolve and divide while others grow and get reinforced by multiple condensins.
source: During the following 'maturation stage', due to condensin exchange some loops dissolve and divide while others grow and get reinforced by multiple condensins (Goloborodko et al., 2015; Alipour and Marko, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation observations and citations to prior work.

claim: The maturation stage takes several rounds of condensin exchange.
source: By the end this stage, which takes several rounds of condensin exchange, the rates of loop death becomes equal the rate of loop division and the chromosome achieves a steady state.
evidence: The claim is based on simulation observations.

claim: Chromosomes rapidly attain a condensed 'noodle'-like shape in early prophase, then spend the rest of prophase growing thicker and shorter.
source: These dynamics are in accord with the observation that chromosomes rapidly attain a condensed 'noodle'-like shape in early prophase, then spend the rest of prophase growing thicker and shorter (Yunis, 1981; Sumner, 1991; Kireeva et al., 2004; Schwarzacher, 1976) (see Discussion).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental observations.

claim: Loop extrusion and strand passing lead to spatial segregation and disentanglement of sister chromatids.
source: We find that the activity of loop-extruding condensins in the presence of topo II leads to compactions of each of the sister chromatids into prophase-like 'noodle' structures (Video 3). Moreover, we observe that formed compact chromosomes (a) become segregated from each other, as evident by the drastic growth of the mean distance between their backbones (Figure 3A), and (b) become disentangled, as shown by the reduction of the winding number of their backbones (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 3A, 3B, and Video 3.

claim: Loop extrusion and strand passing fold highly catenated sister chromatids into separate disentangled structures.
source: Thus, loop extrusion and strand passing fold highly catenated sister chromatids into separate disentangled structures. (Figure 3C, Video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 3C and Video 3.

claim: Compaction, segregation and disentanglement of sister chromatids are highly reproducible and robust to changes in simulation parameters.
source: Despite stochastic dynamics of condensins, compaction, segregation and disentanglement of sister chromatids are highly reproducible and robust to changes in simulation parameters. Disentanglement and segregation were observed in each of 16 simulation replicas (Video 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data across 16 replicas shown in Video 4.

claim: Chromatid segregation and disentanglement occur irrespective of fiber parameters and size of a single condensin molecule.
source: We also performed simulations with altered chromatin polymer parameters (Video 5). Again, we observed chromatids segregation and disentanglement irrespective of fiber parameters and size of a single condensin molecule.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data with varied parameters shown in Video 5.

claim: Condensin abundance on the chromosome significantly affects geometry of simulated chromatids.
source: First, in agreement with the published literature (Savvidou et al., 2005; Steffensen et al., 2001; Hagstrom et al., 2002; Ono et al., 2013) the abundance of condensins on the chromosome significantly affects geometry of simulated chromatids (Video 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data in Video 6 and citations to experimental literature.

claim: Condensin depletion leads to a systematic three-fold increase in chromosome diameter.
source: When we varied abundance of chromosome-bound condensin by 20-fold (five-fold decrease and four-fold increase) we observed two major effects (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). First, we noticed that condensin depletion leads to a systematic (three-fold) increase in chromosome diameter.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both five-fold increase and four-fold decrease of condensin abundance lead to about two-fold drop in linear compaction.
source: Second, we observed nonmonotonic changes in the linear density of chromatin in compacted chromosomes: both five-fold increase and four-fold decrease of condensin abundance lead to about two-fold drop in linear compaction (i.e. two-fold increase in chromosome length).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data.

claim: Reduction of topo II activity prevents disentanglement and segregation of sister chromatids.
source: In these simulations, segregation of sister chromatids is drastically slowed down (Video 7). This effect of topological constraints on kinetics of compaction and segregation is expected since each chromosome is a chain with open ends that thus can eventually segregate from each other. Reduction of topo II activity (increase of the crossing barrier) prevents disentanglement and segregation of sister chromatids, while having little effect of diameter of individual chromatids (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Video 7 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Topo II is essential for rapid chromosome segregation and disentanglement.
source: We conclude that topo II is essential for rapid chromosome segregation and disentanglement, in accord with an earlier theoretical work (Sikorav and Jannink, 1994) and with experimental observations (Wood and Earnshaw, 1990; DiNardo et al., 1984; Newport and Spann, 1987; Shamu and Murray, 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data and citations to theoretical and experimental work.

claim: Interference with cohesin removal or cleavage leads to compaction into elongated chromosomes that fail to segregate.
source: It is known that cohesins are actively removed from chromosomal arms in prophase. Interference with processes of cohesins removal or cleavage leads to compaction into elongated chromosomes that fail to segregate (Kueng et al., 2006; Gandhi et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental observations.

claim: If cohesins remain uncleaved on sister chromatids, compaction occurs but chromatids remain unsegregated.
source: If cohesins remain uncleaved on sister chromatids (Video 8), we observe compaction of sister chromatids, that remain unsegregated, in agreement with experiments (Kueng et al., 2006; Gandhi et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data in Video 8 and citations to experimental observations.

claim: Loop extrusion is sufficient to compact, disentangle and segregate chromosomes from an open interphase state to a compacted, elongated prophase state.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that loop extrusion is sufficient to compact, disentangle and segregated chromosomes from a more open interphase state, to a compacted, elongated and linearly organized prophase state.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results presented.

claim: A dense array of extruded loops makes a chromosome acquire a bottle-brush organization with loops forming side chains of the brush.
source: A dense array of extruded loops makes a chromosome acquire a bottle-brush organization with loops forming side chains of the brush.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the simulation results based on polymer physics.

claim: Polymer bottle-brushes have been studied in physics both experimentally and computationally.
source: Polymer bottle-brushes has been studied in physics both experimentally and computationally (Birshtein et al., 1987; Ball et al., 1991; Li and Witten, 1994), and has been proposed as models of mitotic and meiotic chromosomes (Marko and Siggia, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to polymer physics literature.

claim: Excluded volume interactions and maximization of conformational entropy lead to repulsion of loops from each other.
source: Central to properties of chromosomal bottle-brushes are excluded volume interactions and maximization of conformational entropy that lead to repulsion of loops from each other (Marko and Siggia, 1997; Zhang and Heermann, 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on polymer physics principles and supported by citations.

claim: Loops stretch from the core and extend radially, similar to stretching of side chains in polymer bottle-brushes.
source: Loops further stretch from the core and extend radially (Figure 4), similar to stretching of side chains in polymer bottle-brushes (Birshtein et al., 1987; Ball et al., 1991; Li and Witten, 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data in Figure 4 and citations to polymer physics literature.

claim: Strong steric repulsion between loops stretches the core, maintaining linear ordering of loop bases along the genome.
source: Strong steric repulsion between the loops, caused by excluded volume interactions, stretches the core, thus maintaining linear ordering of loop bases along the genome (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is based on simulation observations shown in Figure 2C and polymer physics reasoning.

claim: Repulsion between loops leads to stiffening of the formed loop-bottle-brush.
source: Repulsion between loops also leads to stiffening of the formed loop-bottle-brush, as chromosome bending would increase overlaps between the loops.
evidence: The claim is based on polymer physics reasoning about the consequences of loop repulsion.

claim: Steric repulsion between loops of sister chromatids leads to chromatid repulsion and segregation.
source: Steric repulsion between loops of sister chromatid leads to segregation of sister chromatids that minimizes the overlap of their brush coronas (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is based on simulation observations shown in Figure 4B and polymer physics reasoning.

claim: When excluded volume interactions are turned off, chromosomes do not assume a bottle-brush morphology and do not segregate.
source: To test this mechanism we performed simulations where excluded volume interactions have been turned off (Video 5). In these simulations, chromosomes did not assume a 'bottle-brush' morphology and did not segregate, which confirms the fundamental role of steric repulsion for chromosome segregation.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Video 5.

claim: Chromosomal compaction by loop extrusion generates the major features of chromosome reorganization observed during prophase.
source: Our results show that chromosomal compaction by loop extrusion generates the major features of chromosome reorganization observed during prophase (Nasmyth, 2001; Alipour and Marko, 2012).
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion supported by simulation results and citations.

claim: Loop extrusion leads to lengthwise compaction and formation of cylindrical, brush-like chromatids, reducing chromosome length by roughly 25-fold.
source: Loop extrusion leads to lengthwise compaction and formation of cylindrical, brush-like chromatids, reducing chromosome length by roughly 25-fold, while at the same time removing entanglements between separate chromatids.
evidence: The claim is based on simulation results.

claim: Loop-extrusion exclusively forms bridges between loci of the same chromosome.
source: Unlike models of prophase condensation based on crosslinking of randomly colliding fibers (Zhang and Heermann, 2011; Cheng et al., 2015), chromatid compaction by loop extrusion exclusively forms bridges between loci of the same chromosome (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is based on the model design shown in Figure 1A and contrasted with other models.

claim: Loop-extrusion in bacteria, mediated by SMC proteins, forms intra-arm chromosomal bridges leading to lengthwise chromosome compaction.
source: Similarly, loop-extrusion in bacteria, mediated by SMC proteins, was suggested to form intra-arm chromosomal bridges leading to lengthwise chromosome compaction (Wang et al., 2015; Wilhelm et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on bacterial chromosome organization.

claim: It takes an extended period of time for loop-extruding enzymes to maximally compact chromosomes.
source: Our computations indicate that it takes an extended period of time for loop-extruding enzymes to maximally compact chromosomes.
evidence: The claim is based on simulation results.

claim: Maximal compaction is achieved by slow maturation of the loop array over multiple rounds of condensin exchange.
source: Maximal compaction is achieved by slow maturation of the loop array over multiple rounds of condensin exchange, rather than a single round of loop expansion.
evidence: The claim is based on simulation results.

claim: It should take about 17 min to achieve maximal compaction, which roughly agrees with the duration of prophase in human cells.
source: Assuming that condensin II in prophase exchanges with the fast rate of condensin I in metaphase (~200 s) (Gerlich et al., 2006) and using an average loop size of 100 kb, and an average spacing of condensins of 30 kb, it should take ~5 condensin exchange times, or about 17 min to achieve maximal compaction, which roughly agrees with the duration of prophase in human cells (Mora-Bermúdez et al., 2007; Leblond and El-Alfy, 1998).
evidence: The claim is based on calculations using simulation parameters and cited experimental data.

claim: Gradual compaction may explain why chromosomes of cells arrested in metaphase continue shrinking for many hours after the arrest.
source: This gradual compaction also may explain why chromosomes of cells arrested in metaphase continue shrinking for many hours after the arrest (condensin II metaphase exchange time ~hours (Gerlich et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on simulation results and cited experimental observations.

claim: The model does not fully capture the specifics of later stages of mitosis.
source: First, our model does not fully capture the specifics of later stages of mitosis.
evidence: This is an explicit limitation stated by the authors.

claim: The model only describes the action of condensin II in prophase.
source: We model only the action of condensin II in prophase (Hirota et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a model limitation stated by the authors with citation.

claim: In metaphase, cells use additional mechanisms of lengthwise (axial) compaction.
source: Simple geometric considerations, Hi-C studies and mechanical perturbation of mitotic chromosomes show that, in metaphase, cells use additional mechanisms of lengthwise (axial) compaction.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple types of evidence.

claim: Loop extrusion does not require specific interaction sites and is therefore robust to mutations and chromosome rearrangements.
source: Loop extrusion does not require specific interaction sites (e.g. loop anchors or condensin binding sites) and is therefore robust to mutations and chromosome rearrangements.
evidence: The claim is based on the model design and logical inference.

claim: A large segment of chromatin inserted into a chromosome of a different species can be reliably compacted by mitotic machinery of the host.
source: This robustness also explains how a large segment of chromatin inserted into a chromosome of a different species can be reliably compacted by mitotic machinery of the host (Dietzel and Belmont, 2001; Hirano and Mitchison, 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental observations and explained by the model.

claim: The diameter and length of simulated chromosomes depend on chromatin fiber properties as well as numbers of condensins.
source: At the same time, this model allows the morphology of mitotic chromosomes to be tuned. Most importantly, the diameter and length of the simulated chromosomes depend on chromatin fiber properties as well as numbers of condensins (Figure 2—figure supplement 1); those dependences invite experimental tests.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loop extrusion is a highly robust mechanism to compact, segregate and disentangle chromosomes.
source: In summary, we have shown that loop extrusion is a highly robust mechanism to compact, segregate and disentangle chromosomes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all simulation results presented.

claim: Loop extrusion by cohesin could lead to formation of interphase topological association domains (TADs).
source: In a recent study (Fudenberg et al., 2015) we also demonstrated that loop extrusion by another SMC complex, cohesin, could lead to formation of interphase topological association domains (TADs).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: During interphase, cohesins are sparsely bound, extruding 50–70% of DNA into highly dynamic loops.
source: We suggest that during interphase, cohesins are sparsely bound, extruding 50–70% of DNA into highly dynamic loops, while metaphase condensins are bound more densely and more processive forming a dense array of stable loops.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their modeling work.

claim: Metaphase condensins are bound more densely and more processive than interphase cohesins, forming a dense array of stable loops.
source: We suggest that during interphase, cohesins are sparsely bound, extruding 50–70% of DNA into highly dynamic loops, while metaphase condensins are bound more densely and more processive forming a dense array of stable loops.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their modeling work.

claim: Loop extrusion can be a universal mechanism of genome folding, to mediate functional interactions during interphase and to compact during mitosis.
source: Taken together these studies suggest that loop extrusion can be a universal mechanism of genome folding, to mediate functional interactions during interphase and to compact during mitosis.
evidence: This is a broad hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their modeling studies.

claim: The model does not rely on a connected 'scaffold'.
source: However, it should be noted that our model does not rely on a connected 'scaffold', and that cleavage of the DNA will result in disintegration of the entire structure, as is observed experimentally (Poirier and Marko, 2002).
evidence: This is a model property stated by the authors and supported by citation to experimental observations.

claim: Formed loops are stably maintained by condensins despite their constant exchange with the nucleoplasm.
source: First, the model shows that formed loops are stably maintained by condensins despite their constant exchange with the nucleoplasm (Hirano and Mitchison, 1994; Gerlich et al., 2006; Oliveira et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results and citations to experimental observations.

claim: Stability of loops is achieved by accumulation of several condensins at a loop base.
source: This stability is achieved by accumulation of several condensins at a loop base (Goloborodko et al., 2015; Alipour and Marko, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results and citations to prior modeling work.

claim: Each loop persists for times much longer than the residency time for individual condensins.
source: Supported by multiple condensins, each loop persists for times much longer than the residency time for individual condensins (Goloborodko et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results and citation to prior work.

claim: A chain of loops naturally assumes a cylindrical shape, with loops forming the periphery and loop-extruding condensins at loop bases forming the core.
source: Second, our polymer simulations show that a chain of loops naturally assumes a cylindrical shape, with loops forming the periphery of the cylinder and loop-extruding condensins at loop bases forming the core (Figure 2C, Video 2), as was predicted in Nasmyth (2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2C and Video 2, and citation to prior prediction.

claim: Condensin-staining experiments reveal cores in the middle of in vivo and reconstituted mitotic chromosomes.
source: Condensin-staining experiments reveal similar cores in the middle of in vivo and reconstituted mitotic chromosomes (Maeshima et al., 2005; Maeshima and Laemmli, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental observations.

claim: Condensin cores appear as early as late prophase in experiments.
source: In agreement with experiments where condensin cores appear as early as late prophase (Kireeva et al., 2004), we observe rapid formation of condensin core in simulations (Figure 2, Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to experimental observations and simulation data.

claim: The structure of chromosomes compacted by loop extrusion is consistent with the loop-compaction picture of mitotic and meiotic chromosomes.
source: Thus, the structure of chromosomes compacted by loop extrusion is consistent with the loop-compaction picture of mitotic (Paulson and Laemmli, 1977; Maeshima and Laemmli, 2003; Marsden and Laemmli, 1979) and meiotic chromosomes (Liang et al., 2015; Kleckner, 2006).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on simulation results and citations to experimental observations.

claim: A recent study suggested a bottle-brush organization of centromeres in yeast, where centromere chromatin loops lead to separation of sister centromeres.
source: A recent study also suggested a bottle-brush organization of centromeres in yeast, where centromere chromatin loops lead to separation of sister centromeres and create spring-like properties of the centromere in mitosis (Lawrimore et al., 2015; 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent experimental work.

claim: The simulations use 1000 condensins per 30 Mb chromosome, as measured experimentally.
source: In our simulations, we use the separation of 30 kb (1000 condensins per 30 Mb chromosome, as measured in Fukui and Uchiyama (2007) and the processivity of 830 kb such that condensins form a dense array of gapless loops with the average loop length of 100 kb, which agrees with available experimental observations (Paulson and Laemmli, 1977; Earnshaw and Laemmli, 1983; Naumova et al., 2013; Jackson et al., 1990).
evidence: The claim is a model parameter based on cited experimental measurements.

claim: The simulations use condensin processivity of 830 kb such that condensins form a dense array of gapless loops with average loop length of 100 kb.
source: In our simulations, we use the separation of 30 kb (1000 condensins per 30 Mb chromosome, as measured in Fukui and Uchiyama (2007) and the processivity of 830 kb such that condensins form a dense array of gapless loops with the average loop length of 100 kb, which agrees with available experimental observations (Paulson and Laemmli, 1977; Earnshaw and Laemmli, 1983; Naumova et al., 2013; Jackson et al., 1990).
evidence: The claim is a model parameter chosen to match cited experimental observations.

claim: Initially, chromosomes are compacted to the density of chromatin inside the human nucleus and topologically equilibrated.
source: Initially, chromosomes are compacted to the density of chromatin inside the human nucleus and topologically equilibrated, thus assuming an equilibrium globular conformation, corresponding to a chromosomal territory.
evidence: This is a description of the initial conditions in the simulations.

claim: In simulations of sister chromatid segregation, the second chromatid traces the same path as the first at a distance of 50 nm and winds one full turn per 100 monomers (60 kb).
source: In the simulations of sister chromatid segregation, the initial conformation of one chromatid is generated as above, while the second chromatid traces the same path at a distance of 50 nm and winds one full turn per 100 monomers (60 kb).
evidence: This is a description of the initial conditions in the simulations.

claim: The initial state of two chromatids running parallel and highly entangled represents the most challenging case for segregation.
source: In this state, two chromatids run parallel to each other and are highly entangled, while residing in the same chromosome territory. This represents to the most challenging case for segregation of sister chromatids.
evidence: This is a statement about the simulation design choice.

claim: The model uses OpenMM, a high-performance GPU-assisted molecular dynamics API.
source: To perform Langevin dynamics polymer simulations we use OpenMM, a high-performance GPU-assisted molecular dynamics (API Eastman and Pande, 2010; Eastman et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a description of the computational methods with citations.

claim: The simulations use a soft-core potential for interactions between monomers to allow chain passing, representing activity of topoisomerase II.
source: To allow chain passing, which represents activity of topoisomerase II, we use a soft-core potential for interactions between monomers, similar to Naumova et al. (2013), Le et al. (2013).
evidence: This is a description of the model design with citations to similar approaches.
